claim: Indian Railways classifies its track in three gauge classes with four widths: broad 1.676 m, metre 1.000 m, and narrow 0.762 m and 0.610 m. Our arithmetic: the broadest is 2.75 times the narrowest, 1,066 mm wider.

evidence.quote: classified by Gauges as Broad (1.676m.), Meter (1.000m) and Narrow (0.762m. & 0.610m)

notes: Ratio and difference: method/gauge_numbers_output.txt ('broad / narrowest = 2.75', 'broad - narrowest = 1066 mm'); label 'our measurement'. So the pitch's 'three widths' is really three classes, four widths.

claim: The multi-gauge classification is still current: a Government of India backgrounder of 15 April 2026 lists broad, metre and narrow gauge in the present tense (and adds standard gauge, 1.43 m).

claim: Broad gauge (5 ft 6 in) was used for the first lines; metre gauge was officially adopted as a second standard in 1871; still narrower gauges were used for developing poor areas and feeding goods to the main railways.

gauges even narrower than the metre gauge

claim: Project Unigauge was launched on 1 April 1992 to convert metre and narrow gauge to broad gauge; by February 2007 the Ministry of Railways said over 13,000 km had been converted and called it a leap towards 'one country, one gauge'.

evidence.quote: Unigauge was launched on April 1, 1992 to develop the backward regions
over 13000 km of metre gauge and narrow gauge have been converted to broad gauge networks

notes: S03 is the Ministry's own celebratory feature before the 2007 Rail Budget: it gains from a large number; '13000 km' is dated Feb 2007, say 'by 2007'. Slogan quote: 'one country, one gauge'.
